PC: *Define misbehavior.* Residents should ask the parent to define the undesirable behavior that resulted in the ‘*popping*.’ Often times the undesired behavior is completely normal behavior for a child of that age. A parent who is not knowledgeable about typical toddler behaviors may mistakenly think that their child is ‘*misbehaving all the time,’* which results in a lot of stress, anxiety, and unnecessary corrective behaviors.[5](#_ENREF_5)

*Time Out*.[6](#_ENREF_6) In this scenario, the parent was unsuccessful at implementing “*Time Out* (TO).” The resident should ask the parent to describe, in detail, how they carried out TO. TO involves removing positive re-enforcement. That is, the parent should take away something that the child enjoys or thinks is fun. Generally, parents remove all stimulation by sending a child to a corner where they are ignored; however, other methods may be used for TO. For example, one can place an enjoyable activity or object on time out (e.g. *“I’m putting the TV on time out,”* or *“I’m putting your toys on time out”*). TO should take place consistently, every time the child performs the undesired behavior. TO is akin to *classical conditioning*, and if it is not performed consistently, the undesired behaviors will not become extinguished. The child should be warned that a TO may take place if they continue to misbehave, thus providing the child with opportunity to grow by making an important decision: *“Do I continue misbehaving and risk having to go to TO, or should I behave.”* If the child continues to misbehave, TO should be given (approximately 1 minute for every year of age beginning at age 2). Before implementing TO, the parent should tell the child (1) exactly what they did wrong to deserve this punishment, (2) that the parent does not like that the child acted this way, and (3) that behavior is the reason why the child is being put in TO. After TO is completed, the parent should reaffirm that the behavior was not appreciated and if done again the child will experience another TO. The caregiver needs to know that the behaviors may get worse before they get better.

*Approach to disciplining a very young, non-verbal child*.[6](#_ENREF_6) Since very young (but mobile) children may not yet understand the nuances of TO, it may be best to apply other strategies. First, consider using *Distraction*. For example, the parent can use a toy to pull their attention away from the undesired behavior. Importantly, this strategy avoids using the word “*no*” and therefore preserving the effectiveness of the word ‘*no’* for future situations (like those that pose a safety risk). Second, child-proofing is a passive and low stress way to prevent ‘misbehavior’ by making specific objects inaccessible to the child. Again, this eliminates the need for the parent to use the word ‘no’ and minimizes the opportunity for parental frustration.
MK: *Corporal punishment teaches young children to manage problems through aggression.*[*6*](#_ENREF_6)In many ways this can be the beginning of a lifetime of violent and/or aggressive behavior. Studies have demonstrated that children who are disciplined with corporal punishment are generally more aggressive than children who do not receive corporal punishment.[7](#_ENREF_7) Furthermore, adolescents who have been injured by community violence are more likely to have been disciplined physically than adolescents who have never been injured by violence.
SBP: The pediatrician should have a clear understanding of the signs of child abuse and the proper ways to document abuse and when it is necessary to call Child Protective Services. Whether or not the *“popping”* fits the legal definition of child abuse, the pediatrician should have a clear understanding of the extent of the physical nature of the discipline. This is best done by making the simple statement, *“A lot of parents tell me that this is a difficult age because the children are so active. Tell me, what do you do when your child is misbehaving?”* In Pennsylvania, corporal punishment is not considered child abuse unless an object is used and/or it causes moderate to severe pain (as exemplified by bruising or scaring).
ICS: *Empathy*. The pediatrician should be seen as an ally to the parent. The pediatrician should acknowledge that raising a 2-year old can be difficult and frustrating. It is important for the parent to realize that the pediatrician is *“on their side.”* Building a strong report will allow the pediatrician to gather further information from the parent regarding the exact nature of her frustration.

*Normalize the parents’ thoughts and emotions*.[6](#_ENREF_6) Explain to the parent that it is reasonable to be frustrated with their child and to even have thoughts of shaking or hitting their child. While these thoughts are common and understandable during times of stress, acting on them is not. By normalizing these thoughts the physician may relieve a great deal of anxiety, self-doubt, and stress for the parent. The next step for the pediatrician and the parent is to brainstorm ideas for non-physical ways to discipline the child.

*Brainstorm*. Have the parent come up with ideas of how to discipline their child besides “*popping*.” The pediatrician might say something along the lines of, *“how do you feel after you pop your child?”* If the parent discloses that they feel guilty, the resident might follow up with a statement like, *“If it makes you feel guilty then perhaps we need to think of something else that doesn’t make you feel so bad. Can you think of some other ways to discipline your child?”*

*“Popping*.” The resident should inquire about what exactly the parent means by the term “*popping*.” Parents from different cultures will use different terminology to describe corporal punishment. Many parents will not use the word, “hit” because of its negative connotation and association with child abuse. Other terminology used by parents includes, *spank, powpow (*some Latino families*),* and *whip.*

*Frustration is the number one factor associated with parental use of corporal punishment.* The parental stress level from work, relationships, finances and health, rather than the child’s behavior, is often the primary factor that leads to this behavior. Assist the parent in identifying and minimizing the underlying causes of their stress.

*Trauma Informed Approach.*[*8*](#_ENREF_8) The term ‘trauma-informed’ is a commonly used term in child abuse and violence research and treatment. It suggests that many people are (or were) chronically exposed to violence and stress. Subsequently, they may exhibit inappropriately aggressive or violent behavior in response to normal stimuli. Recognizing this trauma will help the resident identify and address issues related to stress. For example, when speaking with a parent who has just administered corporal punishment to a child, a resident may think to herself, *“What is wrong with this parent?”* A more *trauma-informed* approach would be to think, *“What is going on in this parents’ life right now, or in the past, that makes her think that this behavior is ok?”* Using this approach, the next appropriate statement would be something like, *“it must be really frustrating to have your child running around like this”* or *“you guys (the parents) look really stressed out. Would you mind if I took the child into the other room and give you guys a break?”* or *“I’m sorry that we’ve kept you waiting so long. Can I offer a snack?”* As the acute stress level declines, the resident should talk with the parent about what in their life causes such significant stress and frustration.
